title: NATO's 'Theory of Victory' Ties Drones and AI to Its Eastern Flank — as Moscow Sets a $205B Wartime Budget
subhead: NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich will present a new plan to defeat a Russian incursion using low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI targeting, while Russia's draft 2027 budget raises defense spending to a record ~$205 billion.

sections.heading: NATO Drafts a 'Theory of Victory' Built on Drones and AI
sections.body:
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, US General Alexus Grynkewich, has drafted a strategy dubbed 'Theory of Victory' for defeating a potential Russian attack on the alliance's eastern flank, and will present it in Poland on October 12, according to Bloomberg, which saw an unclassified version of the document. A NATO official confirmed the plan's existence to the Kyiv Independent.

Per the reporting, the concept integrates traditional land forces with new technologies that matured during Russia's war in Ukraine — low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting — under what is described as an Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative. After gaining freedom of manoeuvre, allied forces would seek to destroy Russian command and control to achieve a quick defeat of an incursion. The document explicitly stresses that NATO remains 'purely defensive' and would avoid involuntary provocations, while naming hybrid threats as a core target of deterrence.

A spokesman for Grynkewich, Colonel Martin O'Donnell, declined to discuss details but told reporters the commander's logic is simple: 'maintain NATO's advantage.' Secretary-General Mark Rutte has said there is no indication Russia is preparing a conventional attack, though Europe should brace for sustained hybrid attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: This is rare open disclosure of how NATO actually intends to fight — moving the alliance's doctrine from a heavy-armor defense model toward cheap drones and AI, which is where the procurement money and industrial competition will follow. The Oct 12 unveiling will function as a shopping list as much as a war plan.

sections.heading: Russia's 2027 Draft Budget Raises Defense to a Record ~$205 Billion
sections.body:
Russia's draft federal budget for 2027 allocates a record sum to defense, with reports citing roughly 17.1 trillion roubles (about $202–205 billion) — figures differ slightly between outlets, with MSN citing $202 billion and APA's Moscow bureau reporting $205 billion. That sustains military spending near Cold War-era peaks relative to the economy.

The budget backdrop is a war economy that keeps scaling. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russia now produces up to 130–140 ballistic missiles per month and holds roughly 700 in reserve, per Meta-Defense and other outlets citing Ukrainian officials — a figure that underscores why Western interceptor and air-defense production is being pushed so hard. Zelensky separately flagged Russian jet-powered Geran drones as a growing problem. At the same time, Russia's oil and gas tax revenue reportedly fell about 17 percent in the first nine months of 2026 despite higher crude prices, a pressure point on how long the spending can be sustained.
sections.whyItMatters: Moscow is locking in wartime spending levels for 2027 even as its energy revenue softens — a signal that the Kremlin is planning for a long conflict, and one that keeps NATO's own rearmament math under pressure. The missile-production numbers also reset the bar for how much interceptor output the West needs.

sections.heading: Boeing Wins a $14.7B PAC-3 Seeker Contract to Triple Output
sections.body:
Boeing has received a seven-year contract worth up to roughly $14.7 billion from Lockheed Martin to expand production of seekers for Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors, Defence Industry Europe and Breaking Defense report. The undefinitized award lets Boeing triple seeker output under a framework agreed earlier this year with the US Department of War, and is expected to create hundreds of jobs in the Huntsville, Alabama area.

The seeker is the component that lets the interceptor find, track and engage targets including hostile aircraft and hypersonic, ballistic and cruise missiles. Boeing has invested more than $200 million since 2024 in expanding seeker capacity, including a 35,000-square-foot facility expansion. Related supply-chain moves include a seven-year, ~$4.7 billion PAC-3 MSE propulsion contract to L3Harris, whose two new Camden, Arkansas facilities are due to open in 2027, and separate frameworks with General Dynamics aimed at tripling PAC-3 MSE and quadrupling THAAD interceptor production. Lockheed has also announced plans to integrate PAC-3 MSE with the Aegis combat system at sea.
sections.whyItMatters: The money is flowing to subcomponents — seekers, motors, controls — not just finished missiles, which is the real bottleneck in Western air defense. Tripling seeker supply is the gating factor for how many Patriots allies can field; linking PAC-3 to Aegis would also push the interceptor from a ground-only system into fleet air defense.

sections.heading: Japan Unveils the Type 25, a 1,000 km Stealth Counterstrike Missile
sections.body: Japan has publicly unveiled the Type 25, a stealthy surface-to-ship missile designed to deliver a roughly 1,000 km counterstrike capability, per Meta-Defense. The system represents a tangible output of Japan's shift toward standoff strike under its record defense budget — the same budget The Diplomat examined this week in a piece questioning whether Tokyo can optimize spending of that scale. Japanese outlets and military-watch reporting frame the missile as a counter to expanding Chinese naval reach, alongside separate Japanese work on a Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is converting budget growth into fielded standoff weapons, which changes the balance in the Western Pacific. A domestically built 1,000 km stealth strike missile reduces Tokyo's reliance on US-supplied systems and signals that the counterstrike doctrine debated for years is now hardware.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact Activated: Turkey and Pakistan to Deploy Forces to Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
Turkey and Pakistan agreed to a 'rapid deployment' of troops and military capabilities to Saudi Arabia under their mutual defense alliance — the Mecca Pact — following an emergency meeting in Riyadh on October 5, Middle East Eye and Reuters report. Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Pakistani Deputy PM Ishaq Dar took part. The trio condemned attacks on Saudi territory, including on Mecca and Medina, without naming the Houthis.

The announcement lands as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press a large-scale offensive to retake Houthi-held territory. Pakistan already maintains tens of thousands of troops in the kingdom and recently sent weapons to Aden, per Reuters. Middle East Eye notes the deployment's immediate tactical impact is unclear, but its timing carries heavy symbolic weight — Riyadh securing regional buy-in, from a nuclear-armed Pakistan and a NATO member in Turkey, for its Houthi counter-offensive.
sections.whyItMatters: A NATO member and the Muslim world's only nuclear state publicly tying themselves to Saudi security deepens the region's bloc structure and further isolates the Houthis. It also shows Gulf security increasingly underwritten by a Turkey–Pakistan–Saudi axis rather than US guarantees alone.

sections.heading: European Defense Startups Pull a Record $7.4B — Most of It American
sections.body:
Venture investment in European defense technology companies reached $7.4 billion year-to-date, nearly three times the full 2025 total, according to a report from data provider Dealroom and Resilience Media cited by the LA Times/Bloomberg. For the first time, US investors supplied more capital (47 percent) than European ones (44 percent).

About 40 percent of the year's funding came from just two German drone deals: Quantum Systems raised $1.2 billion (July, including Blackstone) and Helsing announced a $1.8 billion round including California-based Dragoneer. The number of active defense-tech investors doubled to 455 versus 2023. European officials have raised concerns about foreign ownership of critical defense assets, while entrepreneurs counter that weak local capital markets push them across the Atlantic.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's rearmament is now being financed substantially by American capital, creating a dependency the continent's policymakers are openly uncomfortable with. It also means the startup tier — not just primes like Rheinmetall or BAE — is where drone, satellite and autonomy capacity is being built.

sections.heading: Aselsan Books €1.5B in Air-Defense Deals as Türkiye Pushes Exports
sections.body:
Türkiye's Aselsan disclosed two October air-defense contracts totaling about €1.5 billion — roughly €1.01 billion in additional serial-production work for Türkiye's long-range air-defense program (tied to the 'Steel Dome' effort) and a €488.5 million export order to an undisclosed foreign buyer, per Türkiye Today and the company's KAP filing. Analysts note the award sits on top of an order backlog of about $20.4 billion at end-2025, up 46 percent year-on-year.

The contracts cap a steady 2026 stream of air-defense awards for Aselsan, and the company is now eyeing Asia — CEO Ahmet Akyol has set a target of exports reaching 50 percent of revenue by 2030, with reported interest in partnerships with Japan on air defense and underwater drones. Separately, Türkiye has supplied Ukraine with a small batch of Korkut anti-drone air-defense systems this year, which Kyiv tested in combat and now wants more of, according to Middle East Eye, Türkiye Today and Report.az.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye is converting its NATO-member status and combat-proven hardware into export share, moving up the value chain from drones and armored vehicles into long-range air defense. The Korkut combat feedback loop with Ukraine is effectively free marketing for Ankara's counter-drone line.

bottomLine: Two things happened today that frame the week: NATO's top commander put on paper a plan to fight and beat a Russian incursion using drones and AI, while Moscow's draft 2027 budget pushed defense spending to a record ~$205 billion — offense and defense both scaling up in parallel. Washington kept stuffing the interceptor supply chain, with Boeing's $14.7B PAC-3 seeker deal aimed squarely at the production bottleneck limiting Western air defense. Meanwhile the map of who arms whom is shifting: Japan unveiled a domestic 1,000 km stealth strike missile, Turkey and Pakistan moved to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, and Aselsan and Europe's startup ecosystem showed that the money — American money, increasingly — is chasing capacity outside the traditional primes. NATO's real test is not the strategy document but whether it can buy and build at the pace the new Russian budget implies.
sources: Bloomberg (via Kyiv Independent, Straits Times, United24), Kyiv Independent, MSN/Indian Express, APA.az, Meta-Defense, Defence Industry Europe, Breaking Defense, Lockheed Martin/Boeing statements, The Diplomat, Middle East Eye, Reuters, Türkiye Today, Report.az, AInvest, LA Times/Bloomberg, Dealroom/Resilience Media report, The War Zone
